item.title: Kinosaki Winter Crab: Matsuba Snow Crab Feasts — Guide
item.description: Between November and March, the hot spring town of Kinosaki turns into one of Japan’s great eating destinations. The Sea of Japan just to the north yields matsuba-gani, the male snow crab landed at nearby ports and tagged by port of origin, and the town’s ryokan build entire multi-course dinners around a single crab: sashimi of translucent raw legs, legs grilled over charcoal until the shell blisters, whole boiled crab, a simmering hotpot, and finally rice porridge cooked in the broth.

item.title: The Kasumi Coast: Sea Cliffs and Caves of the San'in Geopark — Guide
item.description: The Kasumi coast, on the Sea of Japan shore of northern Hyogo, is the finest coastal scenery in the prefecture and part of the San’in Kaigan UNESCO Global Geopark. Millions of years of volcanic rock and relentless northern swell have carved the shoreline into columned cliffs, arches, sea caves and pine-topped islets standing in strikingly clear green water. Small sightseeing boats thread among them from the fishing harbour, clifftop paths link viewpoints along the shore, and the same port that draws visitors in summer lands the snow crab that fills the town’s inns in winter.

item.title: Echizen Misaki Lighthouse: A Dramatic Cliffside Coastal Lighthouse — Guide
item.description: Echizen Misaki Lighthouse sits perched on rugged cliffs at the tip of the Echizen Peninsula, offering magnificent views of the open Sea of Japan and access to atmospheric coastal walking trails winding along the promontory. The austere beauty of this remote headland, considerably less visited than Fukui’s more famous Tojinbo Cliffs, makes it a good choice for travellers seeking solitude and dramatic seascape photography away from larger crowds. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Echizen, Fukui Hours Always accessible (exterior); lighthouse grounds daylight hours Admission Free Time needed 1–1.

item.title: Tojinbo Cliffs: Dramatic Basalt Formations Along the Sea of Japan — Guide
item.description: Tojinbo is a roughly 1-kilometre stretch of towering basalt cliffs along the Sea of Japan coast, designated a Natural Monument and considered one of only three such large-scale basalt cliff formations in the world, formed over millions of years by volcanic activity and subsequent erosion. Visitors can walk along clifftop paths for dramatic views down to the pounding surf below, or take a short pleasure boat tour that circles beneath the cliffs for a close-up perspective of the towering rock columns from sea level.

item.title: Fukui Nature: Tojinbo Cliffs, Echizen Coast & Mountain Valleys
item.description: Fukui Prefecture sits along Japan’s Sea of Japan coast, a region long overshadowed by the Shinkansen corridors connecting Tokyo, Kyoto, and Osaka. That relative obscurity has proven to be its greatest gift. The coastline here is raw and elemental — black volcanic cliffs dropping into churning grey-green surf, fishing villages wedged between rocky headlands, and shoreline roads where you can drive for thirty minutes without passing another tourist. Inland, ancient cedar forests shelter Zen temples where silence is practiced as a discipline, and interconnected lakes shimmer in colors that shift with the depth and salinity of the water.

item.title: Shimane Nature Guide: Oki Islands UNESCO Geopark & Dramatic Coastlines
item.description: Shimane’s most dramatic nature lies offshore. The Oki Islands sit 60 kilometers out in the Sea of Japan — remote enough that ancient Japan used them as an island of exile for deposed emperors and unwanted nobles. Today the islands are a UNESCO Global Geopark, recognized for geological formations that tell 600 million years of tectonic history. On the mainland, the Shimane Peninsula’s rocky Sea of Japan coast and the inland Sanbe volcanic highlands round out a nature itinerary that rewards travelers willing to move beyond the main shrine circuit.

item.title: Noto Peninsula Road Trip Guide: Senmaida, Wajima & the Sea of Japan Coast
item.description: The Noto Peninsula extends northward from Kanazawa into the Sea of Japan like a finger pointing toward the Korean coast — a narrow strip of land, roughly 60 kilometres from base to tip, whose distance from any large city has preserved a way of life that has disappeared from most of rural Japan. Here, fishing communities still operate according to seasonal rhythms set centuries ago. Traditional farm families maintain the terraced rice paddies that cascade down hillsides to the sea.
